title: Client money to independent committees that backed an official
question: Does a lobbying client’s money reach an official through a committee the official does not control?
finding: 124 links run from a lobbying client or firm, through a committee no candidate controls, to spending in support of a City official or candidate; the givers’ proportional share of that spending comes to $533,828. In 34 links ($306,195) the giver’s lobbyists also reported contacting that official within two years. The largest: DoorDash gave $100,000 to Forward Action SF, Supporting London Breed for Mayor 2024, Sponsored by Abundance Network, which spent $3.2 million supporting London N. Breed in 2024.
how: Contributions from lobbying clients, lobbying firms and registered lobbyists to committees that no candidate controls are paired with what the same committee reported spending in support of a named candidate (Form 460 Schedule D, Form 496, Form 465; the largest of the three is used because they repeat each other), in the same year or the year after. A committee formed to support one candidate that filed none of those forms is credited with its receipts. The share is the giver’s part of the committee’s receipts in those two years, applied to the support spending.
limits: Committees that no candidate controls can take amounts far above what a candidate may accept; the candidate does not control the committee and may not have wanted its help. The proportional share is arithmetic, not a tracing of dollars: money in a committee is not earmarked. Spending against a candidate is left out. Large companies give to such committees for many reasons besides a matter they lobbied on. An official can sponsor or vote for something a donor wants because the official already favoured it; a donor can give to an official because of what the official already stands for.
